title: Only 7% Pass This Oxford Entrance Exam
summary: Connect words, test arguments and follow the clues through a varied reasoning challenge.

landing.intro:
Read the clues. Make the connections.
Put your thinking to the test.

about.body:
Connect words, test arguments and follow the clues through a varied reasoning challenge.

Use the facts, rules and quantities in each question. No specialist university knowledge is required, and there is no speed score. Each checkpoint reflects the topic just completed. The final result combines your answers, with an optional review of the questions you missed.

This independent entertainment challenge is inspired by academic reasoning. It is not an official Oxford admissions test, an assessment of academic potential or a prediction of admission.

steps: Read the clues and choose one answer.
See your topic profile at each checkpoint and continue to a new challenge.
Reveal your overall result, then optionally review the answers you missed.

about.disclaimer: Independent entertainment challenge. Not an official Oxford admissions test and not affiliated with any university.

next.tagline: Small changes in wording can change the whole claim.
Can you follow a rule without adding an assumption?
Numbers bring a different kind of precision.
What must an argument assume to work?
Sometimes the best answer is what we cannot yet know.
A handful of clues can reveal an exact order.
Now turn the same precision towards space.
Which argument still holds when you test it closely?
The final clues combine language, logic and numbers.

oxford-s1q1.question: A map represents a place. A portrait represents a…

oxford-s1q2.question: A chapter is part of a book. A scene is part of a…

oxford-s1q3.question: A thermometer measures temperature. A ruler measures…

oxford-s1q4.question: Which word is closest in meaning to “concise”?

oxford-s1q5.question: Which pair has the same relationship as seed → plant?

oxford-s1q6.question: Which word is the opposite of “expand”?

oxford-s1q7.question: A glossary explains words. An index helps you find…

oxford-s2q1.question: “Not all entries were complete.” What must be true?

answers.a2: At least one entry was incomplete

oxford-s2q2.question: A claim is described as “plausible”. What does that mean?

oxford-s2q3.question: “At most four people may enter.” Which number is allowed?

oxford-s2q4.question: Which sentence reports a measurement rather than an opinion?

oxford-s2q5.question: “The method may help.” Which rewrite preserves the uncertainty?

oxford-s2q7.question: “Only registered guests entered.” What is guaranteed?

oxford-s3q1.question: All poets in a club are readers. Mina is one of those poets. What follows?

oxford-s3q2.question: No green cards are valid. This card is valid. What must be true?

oxford-s3q3.question: If a switch is on, its light is on. The light is off. What follows?

oxford-s3q4.question: Some musicians are teachers. Which is guaranteed?

oxford-s3q5.question: Every sealed envelope has a stamp. This envelope has a stamp. What can you conclude about whether it is sealed?

oxford-s3q6.question: A rule requires both A and B. A is present, B is absent. Is the rule satisfied?

oxford-s3q7.question: All LUM are PAV. No PAV are ZET. Which must be true?

oxford-s4q1.question: A book costs 24 credits after a 20% discount. What was the original price?

oxford-s4q2.question: Two thirds of 27 people choose option A. How many choose it?

oxford-s4q3.question: The mean of 6, 10, 14 and x is 12. What is x?

oxford-s4q4.question: A session begins at 14:35 and lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. When does it finish?

oxford-s4q5.question: A reader covers 30 pages a day. How many pages remain in a 240-page book after 5 days?

oxford-s4q6.question: The ratio of red to blue beads is 2:3. There are 25 beads in total. How many are red?

oxford-s4q7.question: A value doubles, then 6 is added, giving 30. What was the original value?

oxford-s5q1.question: “Keeping the library open for extra hours will allow more visits.” Which assumption directly supports this?

answers.a1: Some people would use the extra hours

oxford-s5q2.question: “This route is shorter, so it will be faster.” Which missing issue matters most?

answers.a1: The travel speeds on the routes
answers.a2: The date the roads were named

oxford-s5q3.question: “The same total work can be finished sooner by adding staff.” Which assumption is needed?

answers.a2: The extra staff can contribute useful work

oxford-s5q4.question: “Our club is popular because all five people I asked like it.” What is the main gap?

answers.a2: Five people can never like a club
answers.a3: Those five may not represent the wider group

oxford-s5q5.question: Which finding weakens “The new lessons alone caused higher scores”?

answers.a4: The lessons had a new title

oxford-s5q6.question: A seller says a product is reliable because it is expensive. What link is missing?

answers.a1: Proof that every product is cheap
answers.a2: The exact lettering on its label
answers.a3: The date of the next holiday
answers.a4: Evidence connecting its price to reliability

oxford-s5q7.question: “The plan worked once, so it will always work.” What is the reasoning problem?

answers.a2: The first success must be false
answers.a3: A plan can work only once
answers.a4: One success does not establish every future case

oxford-s6q1.question: Among 100 people, 70 use the library and 50 attend tutorials. Both or neither are possible. Can the exact overlap be found?

oxford-s6q2.question: A box holds 12 red or blue counters. What extra fact would determine the number of red counters?

oxford-s6q3.question: A headline says “Visits doubled”. Which detail is needed to know the numerical increase?

oxford-s6q4.question: Two classes have average scores of 50 and 80. What is needed to calculate the combined mean?

answers.a1: The order of the class names
answers.a2: The number of students in each class

oxford-s6q5.question: A journey is 180 km long. Which extra fact lets you calculate its duration at a constant speed?

oxford-s6q6.question: A survey says most respondents agree. What should you inspect before generalising to a city?

answers.a1: How many pages the report has

oxford-s6q7.question: A timetable gives a start but no finish. Which fact would let you find the finish?

oxford-s7q1.question: Nia finishes before Omar, who finishes before Pia. Who finishes last?

oxford-s7q2.question: Four books stand in order: A immediately before B, B immediately before C, and C immediately before D. Which is third?

oxford-s7q3.question: Three talks occupy Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. History is before Music; Music is before Art. When is Music?

oxford-s7q4.question: Seats are numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. Rae sits at 4. Sol sits two seats to Rae’s left. Which seat is Sol’s?

oxford-s7q5.question: A is heavier than B. C is lighter than B. Which is heaviest?

oxford-s7q6.question: Only P, Q or R can be chosen. P is excluded. Choosing Q would require a permit, but no permit exists. What remains?

oxford-s7q7.question: Only X, Y and Z are scheduled. X and Y must both precede Z; their own order is unspecified. Which is guaranteed?

oxford-s8q1.question: An arrow points northeast. Turn it 90° clockwise. Where does it point?

oxford-s8q2.question: A mark is at the top-right of a square. Rotate the square 180°. Where is the mark?

oxford-s8q3.question: Move 4 squares left, then 6 right. Where are you relative to the start?

oxford-s8q4.question: Reflect an up-left arrow across a vertical mirror line. Where does it point?

oxford-s8q5.question: Face south. Turn left by 90°. Which direction now?

oxford-s8q6.question: A point at (3, 2) moves 2 units right and 1 unit down. What are its new coordinates?

oxford-s8q7.question: A shape is reflected across the same mirror line twice. Where does it end?

answers.a2: In its original position and orientation

oxford-s9q1.question: Which is a counterexample to “Every square number is even”?

oxford-s9q2.question: A conclusion requires P and Q. Only P is established. What is the careful verdict?

answers.a4: The conclusion is not yet established

oxford-s9q3.question: Which response addresses an argument’s evidence rather than its author?

answers.a2: The author has an unfamiliar name
answers.a4: The sample excludes half the population

oxford-s9q4.question: A study finds that two measures rise together. What alone follows?

answers.a4: They are associated in the data

oxford-s9q5.question: A policy is defended only because it has always been used. What is still missing?

answers.a3: Evidence that it serves the current goal

oxford-s9q6.question: One explanation fits the observations. What would justify ruling out all alternatives?

oxford-s9q7.question: An experiment can produce evidence that would refute a claim. What does that make the claim?

oxford-s10q1.question: Exactly one statement is true. A says “B is true”. B says “A and C are false”. C says “B is false”. Which is true?

oxford-s10q2.question: A fictional course requires Logic at least 80 and Writing at least 70. Ava has 84/68; Bo 79/90; Cy 82/74. Who qualifies?

oxford-s10q3.question: Of 60 people, 40 use A, 35 use B, and everyone uses at least one. How many use both?

oxford-s10q4.question: A quantity rises by 20%, then falls by 20%. Starting at 100, where does it finish?

oxford-s10q5.question: An upward arrow turns 90° clockwise, then reflects across a vertical line. Where does it point?

oxford-s10q6.question: A library changes its hours and visits rise. Which comparison best checks for a seasonal effect?

answers.a2: Its own visits one day after the change only
answers.a3: A similar library with unchanged hours over the same period
answers.a4: The number of letters in its new timetable

oxford-s10q7.question: “All finalists passed a test” and “Some test passers are not finalists” are both true. Which follows?

answers.a3: Passing is necessary but not sufficient to be a finalist
answers.a4: Every test passer is a finalist
